title: Administrative Wage Garnishment
summary:
Two federal rules out today aim to provide stability for veterans and clarity for debt collection. The Department of Veterans Affairs is extending key timelines in its family caregiver program from five to eight years, and the Postal Service is setting clear procedures for wage garnishment hearings.

For veterans and their family caregivers who were already in the VA’s legacy group, the extension means more time before reassessments and a longer transition period—now through 2028. That should help families avoid sudden changes in support and give VA more room to manage reviews without disruptions. The change takes effect right away and doesn’t add new paperwork or impose costs on small businesses.

Some may see downsides. Extending timelines can delay final decisions for families seeking quicker clarity on eligibility. It also prolongs the shift to newer program rules, which may frustrate those who want faster updates. While VA says the broader economic impact is significant enough to analyze, it doesn’t add notable new regulatory costs.

The Postal Service’s new rule spells out how people can challenge the existence or amount of a non-tax debt before wages are garnished. It defines what counts as a debt, how to file, deadlines, when oral hearings happen, and how decisions are made and shared. Hearings can be in person or virtual, and a neutral official weighs the evidence and issues a written decision.

This should benefit both sides. Individuals get a transparent path to be heard, with a record of the process and decision. The Postal Service gains a consistent, streamlined system that aligns with government-wide standards. On the other hand, those who miss deadlines or do not respond could see garnishment move forward, and not every case will get an oral hearing, which may feel limiting to some. Navigating the process can also be challenging for people without representation.

Bottom line: caregivers in the VA’s legacy program get more time and predictability, and postal debt cases get clearer rules. If you’re affected, watch for official notices, track deadlines, and consider getting advice early to protect your rights.
